anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Table structure, partitioning, and indexing do not match workload access patterns, forcing inefficient scans and lookups independent of statistics freshness.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Concurrent transactions compete for mutually incompatible locks, causing blocking chains or deadlocks that throttle throughput.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Free space in data, log, temp, or backup areas approaches exhaustion, leading to allocation failures and stalled writes.

When all three conditions coexist, the database exhibits a compound failure mode: poorly indexed statements fan out to many rows or pages, inflating the lock footprint of every transaction; the resulting long-lived locks generate extensive blocker–waiter chains that back up connection pools. At the same time, bloated table and index structures plus un-ended transactions prevent space reuse, pushing data files, transaction logs, and temp areas toward their capacity limits. Operators may observe a mixture of symptoms—escalating lock-wait time, sudden spikes in full-table scan I/O, deadlock victim errors, autogrow failures, and "out of space" messages—all intertwined and therefore difficult to attribute to a single root cause.

Causally, the design flaw is the first domino: missing or non-covering indexes make each query touch more rows, holding more locks for longer. The enlarged lock scope amplifies contention; blocked or rolled-back transactions remain open, keeping undo and redo segments active and preventing space reclamation. As log files cannot be truncated and tablespaces swell with untouched but still-locked pages, the storage subsystem fills up. Near-full disks slow auto-extension, which in turn lengthens commit processing and prolongs lock duration, further intensifying contention. Thus, deficient physical design, lock manager stress, and dwindling free space form a self-reinforcing loop that rapidly degrades transactional performance and risks outright service interruption.

entry.official_definition: The number of seconds to wait for more data from a source/replica connection before aborting the read.
entry.trigger_condition: A replica waits longer than replica_net_timeout for more data from the source connection.
entry.workload_impact: The replication network read is aborted and the replica considers the connection interrupted.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL replication system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
